extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and readers of British constitutional politics and reformers
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts standards and evaluative criteria for the functioning, composition, and subsidiary roles of the House of Lords (and contrasted functions of the House of Commons) as described in a chapter of a constitutional treatise. Framing is aimed at judging institutional fitness and proposing reforms (e.g., life-peers, abolition of proxies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Merits: independence, position, and leisure to revise
rubrics_metrics.description: The House of Lords has 'independence to revise judicially and position to revise effectually, leisure to revise intellectually' — these are presented as its great merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three qualities (independence, effective position, leisure for intellectual revision) are valuable and make the Lords useful as a revising chamber, but they can be offset by accompanying faults; they should not blind reformers to defects. Use these merits when weighing the value of a second chamber.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active attendance and visible participation
rubrics_metrics.description: The House often exhibits apathy: 'there are perhaps ten peers in the House, possibly only six; three is the quorum for transacting business' and the 'whole House' appearance is often a jest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the House by real attendance and active presence, not by ceremonial appearance. Low attendance and reliance on proxies undermine public confidence; abolition of proxies is recommended to make the House 'a real House.' Committees may compensate but cannot fully replace a genuinely assembled chamber.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity of composition and class representation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Lords are 'too uniformly made up' — mainly landowners with shared interests and inherited opinions, leading them to revise legislation 'exclusively according to the supposed interests ... of that one class.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the chamber represents a range of interests and backgrounds. Uniform class composition risks systematic bias (resistance to the 'modern spirit') and makes the chamber a partial rather than impartial reviser. Reforms should aim to diversify membership to correct class-bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental, impartial critical capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: A revising chamber should be 'a critic who saw what the age did not see' — a supplemental critic able to rectify the errors of the age; the Lords frequently fail at this (example: their judgment on free trade).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the Lords by whether they offer independent, corrective perspectives (supplemental views) rather than merely resisting change from partisan or class grounds. Historical tests (e.g., free trade) reveal when the chamber's criticism is insightful or merely conservative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Average ability and practical business knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: As a hereditary chamber it 'cannot be of more than common ability' on average; many young Lords are 'worse placed for knowing business' and lack practical experience with trade, finance, and administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate members' actual competence in handling substantive business. Practical business knowledge and administrative experience are necessary for revising statutes dealing with trade, finance, and law reform. Reading alone is insufficient; practical experience and exposure matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective committee work as compensatory mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the full House may be lifeless, 'the committees of the Lords ... do a great deal of work, and do it very well.' Much substantive revision happens in committees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the whole assembly is weak, judge the institution also by the quality and diligence of its committees. Strong committee work can partially offset defects in plenary attendance, but it is not a full substitute for a competent, engaged chamber.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of timidity — acting on judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The Lords are often timid and 'afraid of the nation,' suppressing action on their own judgment and damping earnest peers with 'depressing languor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A revising chamber should be willing to act on considered judgment rather than be swayed by fear of public opinion or inert custom. Excess caution—avoiding engagement on seemingly minor clauses—undermines effective revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation of life-peers to inject talent
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed (and rejected) reform to create life-peers would have added 'thirty or forty such men, added judiciously and sparingly as years went on' to provide critics and raise intellectual capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess reforms by whether they allow appointment of able, meritorious individuals (life-peers) irrespective of family/fortune. Life-peers are presented as a near-perfect expedient to supply the supplemental criticism and expertise the Lords lack.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolition of proxies to ensure genuine accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Proxies have enabled slack attendance and an appearance that the House conducts business when it often does not; 'Proxies ought to have been abolished' alongside life-peers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure institutional legitimacy by whether voting and attendance reflect actual participation. Abolishing proxies would improve appearance and reality of deliberation, increasing public belief in the House's authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of judicial and legislative functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The judicial function of the Lords is 'matter of accident' and problematic — having two supreme courts (Privy Council vs. House of Lords Committee) produced inconsistent results; the supreme court should be 'a great conspicuous tribunal' without competitor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate institutional design by ensuring clear separation: legislative chambers should not be hidden seats of supreme judicial power. Consolidation of judicial authority into a single supreme court is advised to avoid conflicting decisions and confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent criticism of the executive
rubrics_metrics.description: The Lords' natural subsidiary function includes 'the faculty of criticising the executive' — an assembly of men with fixed social position and no constituency can be expected to provide independent criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the House by its capacity to offer multi-sided, impartial criticism of government (example: Lord Grey). A multiplicity of able critics (e.g., life-peers) enhances the value of such oversight by supplying varied perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsidiary function as a political pulpit for leisured ministers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Lords gives leisured Cabinet members 'a voice' and 'position' — allowing ministers exempted from Commons toil to speak with authority and dignity in the Upper House.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the chamber effectively provides a platform for senior statesmen to explain policy and to exercise influence without the relentless demands of Commons attendance; life-peers would enlarge this faculty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of atrophy and need for renewal and merit access
rubrics_metrics.description: The real danger to the Lords is 'inward decay' — losing power by atrophy if members neglect duties, remain of one class, and 'its doors are shut against genius that cannot found a family, and ability which has not five thousand a year.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider mechanisms that permit renewal (admitting talent irrespective of birth/fortune) to prevent decline. Institutions must allow access for merit and change to remain effective over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commons as an electoral chamber (choosing and dismissing government)
rubrics_metrics.description: The main function of the House of Commons is electoral: it 'is an electoral chamber; it is the assembly which chooses our president' and it also has the power of dismissal in addition to election.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the Commons primarily by its effectiveness in selecting and sustaining executive leadership and by the continuous interactive relationship between Premier and Commons; legislative output is secondary to maintaining effective government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressive function of the Commons (reflecting public mind)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commons' second function is 'expressive' — to express the mind of the English people on matters before it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the Commons accurately and effectively expresses public opinion and whether representation channels popular views into parliamentary deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching function of Parliament
rubrics_metrics.description: A third function is the 'teaching' function: a great open council of considerable men should alter society for the better by teaching the nation what it does not know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Parliament by its capacity to educate public discourse and clarify complex issues; the deliberative assembly should raise public understanding and morals, not merely transact business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional efficiency over ceremonial dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: The House of Commons' dignified aspect is 'altogether secondary to its efficient use' — it needs to be impressive but its real value resides in its reality and governance capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating parliamentary institutions, prioritize actual effectiveness in governance and management over stately appearances; ceremonial dignity is valuable only insofar as it supports use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for firm leadership and balanced management
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective leadership is necessary: ministers must 'take the lead' and show firmness; a 'minister who succumbs to the House' seldom thrives, and great leaders have firmness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether executives guide the assembly with appropriate firmness and direction rather than pandering; balanced leader-led dynamics between Cabinet and Commons are essential for a healthy system.
